questions.knowledge_point: Approximating a Solution to an Initial Value Problem Using a Tangent Line Approximation
questions.problem:
Consider the initial value problem 

$$
{y}^{′}=x{y}^{2},\,y(1)=2.
$$

Current part:

Find the function $L(x),$ the tangent line approximation of $y(x)$ at $x=1.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $L(x)=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation to $y(x)$ at the point $a=1$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =y(a)+{y}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

From the initial condition, we know that $y(1)=2.$ We also know that ${y}^{′}(x)=x{y}^{2},$ so

$$
{y}^{′}(1)=1\cdot {2}^{2}=4.
$$

Substituting our values for $y(1)$ and ${y}^{′}(1)$ into our expression for $L(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =2+4(x-1) \\  & =2+4x-4 \\  & =4x-2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We'll start with the table from part 3.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $1$ |

We now proceed to approximate $y(\frac{3}{2})$ using Euler's method.

**Step 1.** We compute the values of ${x}_{\text{new}}$ and ${y}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{5}{4} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=2+1=3\end{aligned}
$$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $1$ |
| $\frac{5}{4}$ | $3$ | $$ | $$ |

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =x{y}^{2}=\frac{5}{4}\cdot {3}^{2}=\frac{45}{4} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{45}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{4}=\frac{45}{16} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=\frac{5}{4}+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=3+\frac{45}{16}=\frac{93}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $1$ |
| $\frac{5}{4}$ | $3$ | $\frac{45}{4}$ | $\frac{45}{16}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $\frac{93}{16}$ | $$ | $$ |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(\frac{3}{2})≈\frac{93}{16}.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x{y}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{y} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $y.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{y} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\ -\frac{1}{y} & =\frac{{x}^{2}+2C}{2} \\ \frac{1}{y} & =-\frac{{x}^{2}+2C}{2} \\ y & =-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+2C} \\ y & =-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+K} \\ y & =-2{({x}^{2}+K)}^{-1},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=2C$ is an arbitrary constant.
